answer: Hypothesis: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both the original and the replication studies. Among original–replication pairs (study_data, strict male-majority = >0.5 male authors on BOTH author teams), Economics has the largest share at 55.6% (10 of 18 pairs), followed by Cognitive at 41.1% (99/241) and Social at 30.1% (201/668). The Economics result covers n=18 studies (all from the 'ee' project), so the lead over Cognitive and Social is clear in share but rests on a small sample. The ranking is stable under both robustness checks: with a >= 0.5 lenient threshold (Economics 83.3% vs Social 59.9% vs Cognitive 54.8%) and with id-level aggregation (one pair per original study; Economics 55.6% vs Cognitive 36.7% vs Social 27.0%). Caveat on counting units: the primary row-level count treats each replication lab as its own O/R pair, so highly-replicated Social/Cognitive studies are weighted more heavily than under the id-level count; despite that weighting difference, both units point to Economics as the domain where both original and replication author teams are most often male-majority.

payload.hypothesis: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies: 55.6% (10/18) of original-replication pairs have male-majority author teams on both sides, the largest share across domains (Cognitive 41.1%, Social 30.1%), though based on only 18 Economics studies.
payload.workflow: Loaded study_data (927 rows, 141 studies). Primary: for each discipline, share of O/R pairs (id x lab rows) with authors_male.o > 0.5 AND authors_male.r > 0.5. Robustness: (1) threshold >= 0.5; (2) id-level aggregation (first-lab and mean-male-ratio) with > 0.5. Economics leads under all four variants. Replication_success excluded (no discipline/author-gender columns).
